Behavioral capabilities

Between 12 and 24 months, behavior shows sparks of deliberate, multi-step, symbol-guided action. A 2026 study categorizes children’s object engagement (Figure) 124.

Locomotion becomes an always-on data-collection loop as new walkers cover on the order of two thousand steps and 1̃7 falls per hour during free play 1, vastly expanding active sampling of objects, surfaces, and affordances for learning. Locomotion shifts from wide-based, fall-prone toddling to efficient, planned movement as thousands of daily steps tune balance, stride, and path control–yielding stiff-legged running, stair-climbing with support, kicking, and furniture climbing by  18-24 months 1, 2, 3, 4. The study examines social and environmental context (Figure).

Fine motor control progresses from generic grasps to role-differentiated bimanual manipulation 5, 6 and basic tool use (spoons, rakes, rails, levers) 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, with strengthening hand preference 13, organized scribbles 14, taller block stacks (some can reach up to 8 blocks by 25 months) 15, and increasingly anticipatory action planning (e.g planning for the most comfortable hand/wrist pose when grasping) 16, 17. Tool use and problem solving show emerging analogical transfer: by ∼\sim18-24 months, toddlers who learn an effective strategy for retrieving an out-of-reach toy (e.g., choosing the correct tool from several candidates) transfer that strategy to structurally similar but perceptually different problems, indicating that the world model is beginning to extract and reuse abstract relational structure from specific episodes rather than remaining bound to surface features 18. Similarly, action understanding becomes more latent-goal-based in this period. By 18 months, toddlers can reproduce what an adult intended to do even when the adult visibly fails, indicating that the child’s model distinguishes the observed movement from the unobserved goal state it was meant to achieve 19. More broadly, selective-imitation findings from the second year show that young children do not simply copy surface behavior; they increasingly treat others’ actions as means chosen under constraints, copying unusual means preferentially when those means appear necessary or rational rather than arbitrary 20. The study estimates changes in material engagement with age (Figure).

Mobility feeds language and concept learning: head-mounted camera studies show that naming often occurs during brief, toddler-created "clean views" of a single object, and words learned at those moments stick better than labels delivered in cluttered scenes 21. Expressive vocabulary and early compositionality accelerate: by 18-24 months toddlers have learned 50-100 words 22, 23, and most children are combining two words ("more milk") 24. This vocabulary acceleration co-occurs with a broader restructuring: it coincides with a categorization spurt–a sharp increase in spontaneous sorting behavior (e.g., exhaustively grouping objects by kind) that emerges around 18 months 25, 26. Similarly, toddlers increasingly exploit heuristics such as mutual exclusivity by  17 months (e.g when presented a familiar and a novel object (e.g. car and phototube) and asked to "look at the dax", 17-month-olds increased looking to the novel object (i.e. phototube) above baseline preference) 27 and a growing shape bias (toddlers start to assume that nouns refer to objects of a particular shape rather than to their color, texture, or size) from  18-24 months to generalize names 28. They also become more "symbol-minded" in a general sense: many can learn from pictures as referential symbols by 18-24 months 29 even as scale-error attempts (e.g., trying to sit in a doll chair) reveal an ongoing integration between perception, action planning, and inhibitory control 30. Basic pretend play with object substitutions (e.g using a "banana" as a "phone") is also common across this window, further signaling the emergence of symbolic thought while enhancing social sensitivity, emotional regulation, and understanding of multi-step narratives 31. This capacity to quarantine simulated states from veridical representations is a foundational precursor to generalized forward planning, hypothetical reasoning, and "theory of mind," allowing the agent to run internal forward models using representations that conflict with immediate sensory input 32, 33. A longitudinal experiment measures early word recognition (Figure) 125. The study uses a second word-recognition task (Figure).

Language in this window becomes increasingly event-structured and combinatorial, not merely lexically larger. By ∼\sim22-24 months, toddlers can use syntax to infer latent event structure: when viewing unseen events paired with spoken sentences, they retain a novel verb’s syntactic frame (e.g "Anna blicked" versus "Anna blicked the baby") over a delay and later use it to constrain their interpretation 34, and 2-year-olds can use syntax alone to infer whether a novel verb refers to a causative versus synchronous relation (i.e causative versus synchronous events) even before seeing the candidate scenes 35. Relatedly, by ∼\sim18 months infants show evidence of representing abstract nonlocal syntactic dependencies (e.g for "What did the chef burn?" knowing the relationship between "What" and "burn"), indicating that the language model is beginning to support structured relations that extend beyond adjacent words 36. This matters for world modeling because language is no longer functioning only as an object-labeling system; it is beginning to specify who did what to whom and what kind of relation links event participants 37. A 2026 reviewed preprint aggregates early word-recognition data (Figure) 126. The 2026 reviewed preprint relates recognition and vocabulary growth (Figure). The analysis examines individual differences over development (Figure).

Language in this window also begins to support displaced reference–the capacity to denote entities and events that are not currently perceivable. By ∼\sim18–24 months, children spontaneously talk about absent objects, past experiences, and anticipated events in conversation with caregivers 38, 39, and even prelinguistic 12-month-olds point to an absent object’s prior location to communicate about it to an uninformed adult, indicating that gestural displaced reference precedes its full linguistic expression 40. This capacity is significant for world modeling because symbolic vehicles can now access and transmit internal world-model states—past episodes, absent objects, anticipated events—entirely decoupled from the ongoing sensory scene. Moreover, language begins to function as a channel for directly updating the world model, not just labeling it. Towards the end of this window, toddlers who are told about a change to a hidden object (e.g., "the doll got wet") update their mental representation accordingly, expecting the transformed state when the object reappears rather than the last directly observed state 41. This demonstrates that verbal testimony can write to the internal world model in the absence of any direct perceptual evidence, marking an early transition from purely experiential to partially testimonial world-model construction. A longitudinal study describes toddler vocalizations and gestures (Figure) 127. The study considers gaze during communicative acts (Figure).

A further representational upgrade in the second year is the emergence of an explicit self-model. During this window, toddlers increasingly recognize their own image, use self-referential forms such as personal pronouns, and show more advanced pretend play, suggesting that the world model now includes the self as a stable referential entity rather than merely the default point of view 42, 43. Importantly, this self-model is still incomplete and dissociable across levels: even as mirror self-recognition emerges, toddlers often struggle to explicitly represent their own body as a size-constrained object in action planning, and this mismatch likely contributes to classic scale errors and other body-planning failures 44, 45. Nonetheless, the emergence of the self-model coincides with the appearance of self-conscious emotions–embarrassment, shame, and pride–which become reliably observable (albeit still rudimentary) around 18-24 months and correlate with the attainment of mirror self-recognition 46, 47, 48, suggesting that the world model now includes not just the self as a referential entity, but a nascent representation of how the self is evaluated by others. In parallel, toddlers begin representing ownership as a social-relational property linking persons to objects. By ∼\sim18–24 months, children use possessive language (e.g., "mine," "daddy’s"), protest when their possessions are taken, and track who held an object first as a cue to ownership 49. This represents a new representational layer in the world model: objects are now encoded not only by their physical properties and functions but by a person-linked relational tag specifying who controls or has prior claim over them—an early step toward modeling social-institutional facts that go beyond physical reality.

The agent model’s state-tracking capacity also deepens during this window. Looking-time paradigms show that 15-month-olds represent an agent’s false belief about an object’s location: they look longer when the agent searches where the object actually is (but the agent should not know this) than when the agent searches at the now-empty location consistent with the agent’s outdated belief 50. This extends the implicit belief-tracking detected earlier (see 6-12 months) to a paradigm in which the infant must predict the agent’s action from a decoupled, counterfactual world state. Complementary evidence from desire understanding shows a parallel advance: 18-month-olds who observe an experimenter expressing disgust toward crackers but delight toward broccoli hand the experimenter broccoli, even though the toddler herself prefers crackers; 14-month-olds, by contrast, egocentrically offer their own preferred food 51. Together, these results imply that by 18 months the world model can decouple another agent’s value function and belief state from the child’s own, supporting richer social perspective-taking. Leveraging these abilities, prosociality comes online in graded form: 18-month-olds readily perform instrumental helping (helping others achieve concrete, goal-directed actions), while empathic and especially costly (altruistic) helping become more reliable closer to the end of the second year 52, 53. Beyond unilateral helping, toddlers also begin engaging in cooperative joint-goal activities: by 18-24 months, pairs of toddlers can coordinate complementary roles to achieve a shared outcome (e.g one child operates one end of a tube apparatus while a partner operates the other), and they actively attempt to re-engage a partner who stops participating—implying a representation of the shared plan and the partner’s necessary contribution 54, 55. Visual perspective taking also becomes behaviorally explicit in this window: by ∼\sim24 months, toddlers demonstrate Level-1 perspective taking–they can determine what another person can vs. cannot see from a different vantage point and use this to guide their own behavior, such as selectively showing or hiding objects 56. This complements the implicit belief-tracking measured by looking time at 15 months; here, the child’s own actions reveal an online computation of another agent’s perceptual access to the world.

The social world model also becomes more epistemic: toddlers begin tracking not only what other agents want or believe, but also which informants are worth learning from. By 18 months, toddlers are less willing to learn a novel word or imitate a novel action from a speaker who has previously labeled familiar objects inaccurately 57. By 24 months, this selectivity is more robust: toddlers preferentially learn novel word-object mappings from previously accurate speakers 58, and can use a third party’s agreement/disagreement gestures (nodding vs shaking) to infer which testimony about an object’s identity or location should be accepted 59. The world model is thus beginning to represent speaker reliability as a latent variable, filtering socially transmitted information by source quality rather than treating testimony as uniformly trustworthy. Related infant experiments test expectations about fair social behavior (Figure) 130. Infants are sensitive to unequal distribution by about 15 months. (Figure).

Spatial navigation shows robust geometric reorientation by  18-24 months with increasing use of landmarks (any salient environmental cues (like a unique object, building, or tree) that can serve as reference points) 60, 61, 62, indicating early integration of layout geometry and features. Beyond geometric reorientation, spatial cognition in this window also shows the emergence of allocentric coding–the ability to represent object locations relative to environmental landmarks rather than to one’s own body. Towards the end of this window, toddlers can use stable external cues to relocate a hidden object even after being passively moved to a new vantage point, indicating that the spatial world model is no longer locked to an egocentric reference frame 63, 64, 65. Relatedly, locomotion becomes more prospective and detour-capable: by ∼18–24 months, toddlers can select efficient detour routes around barriers to retrieve a goal, integrating spatial layout with action planning rather than relying solely on direct approach 66, 3.

Numerical cognition shifts from purely pre-verbal magnitude tracking ("approximate number sense") toward emerging exactness: toddlers show nascent ordinal judgments 67 and begin mapping small number words to precise set sizes 68 (often knowing what "one" (and even "two") means around the 24-month mark 69) and this growth is measurably shaped by caregiver "number talk" during 14-30-month interactions 70. Causal learning becomes more probabilistic by the end of this window: by about 24 months, toddlers can watch two candidate causes produce an effect with different probabilities and then preferentially intervene on the object that was more likely to generate the outcome, even when absolute frequency is controlled 71, suggesting that the world model is no longer restricted to deterministic event schemas or direct trial-and-error learning, but can estimate graded causal strength from noisy evidence. Furthermore, causal modeling in this window builds on the latent-cause inference of the previous window. By 10-12 months infants already infer a hidden agent in certain unseen causal interactions 72, 73. What changes across the second year is that causal inference becomes broader, more observational, and more abstract. By ∼\sim24 months, toddlers can learn causal structure from watching other people’s interventions, distinguishing genuine cause-effect relations from mere temporal association and then intervening on the causal object themselves 74. They also infer unobserved causes for apparently spontaneous physical events in contexts that go beyond the specific hidden-agent launching cues emphasized in the first year (e.g searching for a cause after seeing a toy spontaneously light up) 75. More generally, 18-30-month-olds can extract higher-order relational causal principles from just a few observations and use them to generate or predict novel causal outcomes (e.g understanding that two identical objects must be placed on a toy for it to light up) 76. The shift, then, is not from “visible causation” to “hidden causation,” but from relatively specific hidden-cause expectations to more flexible observational, probabilistic, and relational causal modeling.

Executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, and flexible goal maintenance) move from fragile to reliably measurable across this window. Goal maintenance/working memory improves: by ∼\sim2 years, children can keep track of multiple hidden objects in multilocation search ("Spin-the-Pots") 77, and 24-month batteries show success not only on classic A-not-B-like demands but on invisible-displacement versions with brief delays, indicating that toddlers can maintain a latent object state across occlusion and distraction rather than relying only on the last visible location 78. Inhibitory control also strengthens across paradigms: toddlers increasingly succeed on A-not-B/delayed-response 79 and detour/object-retrieval variants (suppressing the direct reach to a visible goal), with performance falling when tasks require arbitrary multi-step means actions and improving when the task structure is more causally transparent or easier to maintain in working memory 80, 81. Toddlers also begin to tolerate short, structured delays on snack-delay-style tasks 82 as well as crayon- and tongue-delay tasks (i.e not using crayons until the adult returns, and holding a cracker on the tongue without eating it) 78. It is best, however, to keep any flexibility claims conservative: near the end of this window, toddlers can maintain a simple sorting rule over several trials and inhibit competing responses, but full rule switching remains limited, which is why 24-month longitudinal batteries typically use pre-switch rather than post-switch sorting as the informative measure 78. By the end of the second year, then, executive control is still highly task-sensitive, but it is no longer just a collection of isolated successes and failures; it is becoming a coherent, behaviorally expressed control capacity that supports hidden-state maintenance, response suppression, and simple goal-guided action over delay 78.

Episodic memory undergoes major expansion across the second year of life, though retention remains unreliable over long delays. Using elicited-imitation paradigms, 20-month-olds can reproduce multi-step event sequences (including their temporal order) after delays of up to 12 months 83, 84, a dramatic increase from the <1-month retention window typical prior to this period 85, 86. Memory for locations also improves across this window—though still fragile—with evidence that toddlers can retain spatial information across multi-month delays under favorable conditions 84. Nonetheless, retention remains highly incomplete: retrospective studies suggest that even salient events from around 19 months are remembered only ∼40% of the time when children are tested years later (which is, however, likely explained by encoding and forgetting) 87. Consistent with the emerging self-model described above, between ∼\sim18–24 months children also begin referencing themselves in past events, indicating that episodic memory is starting to incorporate the self as a participant in remembered scenes rather than merely storing perceptual episodes 88. Even so, fully autobiographical, narratable recollection remains rudimentary in this period and develops substantially later, helping explain why most episodic memories from the second year of life ultimately fail to persist into later childhood 89, 90, 85. A 2026 preprint examines early hippocampal development (Figure) 129. The preprint models hippocampal trajectories (Figure).

Training data and optimization

sleep increasingly stabilizes and abstracts episodes into nascent semantic/generalized knowledge 91, 92, 93.

From 12-24 months, the optimizer pursues a tight bundle of implicit objectives that each come with distinctive training data and error signals, and together they explain the aforementioned behavioral step-changes. A locomotor calibration objective continuously minimizes sensory prediction error across vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual channels: every footfall, sway, and retinal-slip event supplies supervised error to cerebellar forward models and cortical mismatch units, yielding fewer falls, narrower bases of support, and lawful gains in path planning, stairs, kicking, and early running as "teacher" spikes gate plasticity at co-active synapses. A manipulation/tool-use objective minimizes end-state and trajectory costs: mismatches between intended end-states and achieved configurations (orientation, torque, force) produce vector-like errors on each attempt, while success-contingent dopaminergic bursts stamp in the policies that led to scooping with a spoon, raking, levering, and role-differentiated bimanual coordination; over repetitions, anticipatory grasps emerge because forward models begin to predict the distal pose required for comfort at movement’s end. These motor objectives double as a system-identification loop: by driving down trajectory and end-state errors across thousands of self-generated interactions, the learner is forced to infer latent physical parameters-mass, friction, rigidity/compliance, centers of mass and graspable axes-and to encode affordance constraints like hinges and slots, yielding object concepts that transfer across contexts. In parallel, minimizing locomotor prediction errors over optic flow, vestibular, and proprioceptive cues stabilizes body- and world-centered coordinate frames and carves metric structure for distance, slope, and boundaries, seeding landmark/layout codes and the "intuitive physics" priors that support reorientation and increasingly abstract reasoning about objects.

As sensorimotor primitives solidify, the bottleneck shifts to maintaining latent task state over longer, branchier action sequences while suppressing prepotent reaches; accordingly, a control-and-working-memory objective optimizes cortical-basal ganglia gating so that the right rule stays "on line" and incorrect motor programs are paused. Each failure on a control-reliant task yields conflict signals in dACC and negative TD-errors in striatum that penalize the impulsive policy; the hyperdirect STN pathway transiently raises decision thresholds, while MD-thalamus-PFC loops amplify and stabilize the active goal representation. With practice, neuromodulatory precision control (ACh/NE) reduces distractor gain and sharpens gating selectivity, producing reliable multi-step deferred imitation and short, rule-bound delays by the end of the window.

A symbol-grounding objective maps word-forms to latent causes in the scene, not just pairing "sounds to things" but also exploiting social and perceptual structure to manufacture informative cross-modal contingencies. Joint-attention bouts (adult gaze/point/name) and child-initiated "clean views" create high-confidence alignments between short acoustic tokens and single object files; the learner effectively runs cross-situational expectation-maximization, updating a sparse lexicon that penalizes overlapping mappings (mutual exclusivity) and regularizes by shape-stable visual invariants, yielding the classic shape bias. Pragmatic inference functions as a noisy-channel prior-speaker intent, common ground, and naming timing steer credit assignment-while distributional frames ("more _", "kick the _", "grab two _") provide syntactic-bootstrapping signals that constrain verb meanings and enable early composition despite telegraphic production. Gains in phonological working memory and sleep-dependent spindle-ripple coupling increase retention and interference-resistance, consolidating single-trial labelings into anterior-temporal conceptual codes that transfer across views and media (objects <-> pictures). A longitudinal study relates infant attention to later vocabulary (Figure) 128. The study estimates relationships between attention and vocabulary (Figure).

A spatial reorientation objective reduces discrepancy between predicted layout geometry and landmark relations ("toddler SLAM"): self-motion updates from path integration and head-direction cells are "closed" against extended surfaces whenever predicted pose drifts, forcing the system to anchor geometry (walls, corners, junctions) as the most reliable basis for an allocentric map. Through repeated experience and replay, these geometric codes are combined with feature-based inputs, with stability and distinctiveness determining their weight such that, by  18-24 months, toddlers can fuse geometry and landmarks to recover proper heading direction, recognize locations across viewpoints, and navigate through a sparse graph of corners and gateways transformed between egocentric and allocentric representations.

As the learner’s agent model matures, the objective widens from "reduce my error" to "reduce another’s control error." Observed need or a stalled goal generates other-referenced prediction errors; STS/TPJ parse agents and intentions, ACCg/insula register the gap between expected and achieved states, and vmPFC-striatal critics fold vicarious value into a common currency. Contingent approval and task success provide dense scalar supervision that credits policies which minimize another’s error, shifting behavior from instrumental assistance toward state-oriented empathic responses and, as cost representations sharpen, toward costlier altruistic choices when expected social value outweighs self-cost.

A declarative-binding objective incentivizes the system to preserve the structure of experiences rather than just isolated traces. Every retrieval failure or partial reinstatement acts as supervised feedback, driving hippocampo-cortical updates that sharpen links between items, places, and temporal order. The same comparators that stabilize reorientation maps (e.g entorhinal grid, boundary codes aligned with hippocampal place codes) also provide the coordinate frame for binding "what-where-when" into coherent episodes. Across waking replay and dendritic plateau tagging, recently co-activated representations are selected for offline consolidation, gradually transforming fragile sequences into durable, relationally indexed memories. By late in the second year, this system will support month-scale retention of event sequences and increasingly flexible transfer, as relational bindings become less scene-bound and more transportable across contexts.

Imitation learning functions as a meta-learned objective that amortizes control, perception, and language priors across domains. By repeatedly optimizing to match the outputs of competent demonstrators, toddlers acquire hierarchical action sketches, causal scripts, and pragmatic templates that initialize policy search in new tasks, effectively few-shot policy cloning. One interesting example of this dynamic is 15-month infants’ imitation of adults’ persistence during task execution 94. In general, frontoparietal ’mirror’ circuitry, BG gating, and cerebellar inverse models jointly compress observed sequences into reusable motor-cognitive programs, so subsequent learning starts closer to the optimum and needs only small, task-specific prediction-error adjustments.

Threading these objectives is an intrinsic "learning-progress" objective that steers internalized objectives towards the Goldilocks zone (where prediction errors fall fastest); phasic NE resets policies when models fail, ACh raises the precision on trustworthy sensory errors, and distributional DA calibrates risk and vigor-together scheduling when the system exploits a just-learned controller (e.g., a spoon grip) versus when it perturbs policies to discover cleaner labels or new affordances.

Neural development

Cognitively, this stage of development marks a shift in the child’s world model from mostly sensorimotor predictions to increasingly abstract, relational, and symbolic representations that support flexible generalization and planning. Word learning accelerates and becomes more "model-based": toddlers begin forming a denser lexical-semantic network and adopt efficient inductive biases like the shape bias (organizing objects by shape instead of size, color, or texture), enabling rapid category extension from few exemplars and seeding the classic vocabulary spurt for many children 95, 96. Sleep starts playing a measurable role in consolidating these new words into the lexicon (e.g., emergence of lexical competition only after sleep), consistent with fast hippocampal capture and slower neocortical integration 97. At the same time, probabilistic expectations about events become richer and more coherent (12-month-olds already integrate multiple cues to form Bayesian-like predictions 98) so by the second year children treat causes, agents, and object dynamics as structured variables in a causal model rather than isolated facts.

The toddler’s "physics engine" also becomes more structured: beyond simple contact/no-contact rules, they encode graded support constraints (proportion- and position-of-contact, and by  13 months proportional distribution of mass) 99, begin exploiting material/weight cues for planning 100, and continue to use violations of expectation as catalysts for targeted exploration 101. Object representations extend from visible displacements to robust solutions of invisible-displacement problems by  18-24 months 102, signaling genuine mental tracking of occluded trajectories. Action planning folds advanced physics models back into control: by  14-19 months many children anticipate end-states (e.g., spoon reorientation and efficient grips) 16, 103, and imitation becomes selective and constraint-sensitive (i.e toddlers copy strange actions when they appear rational given the actor’s constraints, otherwise defaulting to more efficient actions 20). Yet characteristic limits still reveal what’s under construction, such as the gravity bias in tube-trajectory tasks near age two, where expectations of straight-down motion can override accurate path visualization 104. Overall, these changes reflect a physics model that is increasingly relational, predictive, and action-useful, tightly coupled to symbolic growth in language and pretend play, and already operating as a compact causal model that supports multi-step, foresighted interaction with the world.

The brain’s large-scale dynamics and wiring take major steps toward fast, high-bandwidth, "segregated-yet-integrated" control over this period. Cortically, oscillatory timing quickens and stabilizes: peak-alpha frequency continues its early rise into the lower alpha range 105 and the aperiodic (1/f) slope flattens nonlinearly through 24 months 106, both pointing to shorter integration windows and tighter excitation-inhibition balance for local selection and prediction. Sleep spindles are bilaterally synchronous by  12-18 mo 107 and slow-oscillation<->spindle coupling that is weak/unsystematic in late infancy becomes reliably positive in toddlers 108, strengthening the hippocampo-cortical channel that abstracts from episodes. A 2026 peer-reviewed study finds stable individualized networks across ages 8–60 months, with language laterality tracking verbal ability (Figure) 123. Behavior-network coupling reorganizes from sensorimotor-anchored to control-network-anchored: at 12 months, walking covaries mainly with motor and posterior default-mode connectivity, but by 24 months it shifts toward dorsal attention and posterior cingulo-opercular (salience/monitoring) circuits 109, evidence that action control is becoming top-down and distributed rather than local and reflexive. Default-mode hubs continue to ramp regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) faster than primary systems, and rCBF increases are tightly coupled to strengthening DMN functional connectivity 110, an explicit perfusion-network link that helps explain the toddler’s DMN consolidation, emerging self-awareness 111, and growing antagonism (and perhaps arbitration) between internal modeling (DMN) and attention systems 112.

The substrate keeps pace: association pathways show steep myelination and axonal-organization gains during the first two years (fractional anisotropy (FA) rises; radial diffusivity (RD) falls; quantitative myelin metrics like R1 increase) 113, with dedicated 1- and 2-year-old DTI/MRI atlases now resolving tract-specific maturation 114, 115; limbic highways critical for spatial (and perhaps non-spatial) navigation and declarative binding (e.g the fornix, parahippocampal cingulum, and uncinate) are among the bundles upgrading conduction and phase-locking fidelity. Macroscopically, total brain volume continues to expand from year one to year two by roughly fifteen percent (about  948 cm³ ->  1072 cm³ in one longitudinal MRI cohort, now at 80% of adult brain size 116), which raises global signaling capacity and energy budget even as white-matter efficiency improves. Synaptic quantities shift in a region-specific way that matches the behavioral profile: in primary visual cortex, the post-natal synaptogenesis burst has already peaked by  8-12 months and the 12-24 month window is dominated by the early phase of pruning (density remains above adult levels but is declining) 117, while in prefrontal cortex synaptic density is still rising beyond  15 months, climbing toward the well-known childhood overshoot that later prunes back 118; dendritic-spine counts in human PFC reach 2-3x adult values in childhood before protracted elimination that may last well into the third decade of life 119. In parallel, hippocampal machinery grows and plugs in: human MRI shows a rapid hippocampal volume increase up to  2 years 120, and resting-state work across infancy into early childhood finds the hippocampus strengthening its coupling to posterior midline DMN nodes that anchor scene/context models 121, aligning with toddlers’ improving allocentric guidance and episodic binding. Thalamo-cortical gateways also mature, with longitudinal infant studies showing system-specific thalamic connectivity (including later-emerging links to DMN) becoming more adult-like by the end of year two 122, complete with cognitive correlations.
